references.text: Isaac sowed in the land and reaped a hundredfold that year, for the Lord blessed him. The motif of a hundredfold yield as a sign of God's blessing.
Parallel passage in Matthew's version of the parable of the sower, where some seed fell on good soil and produced fruit: some a hundred, some sixty, some thirty times what was sown.
Parallel passage in Mark's version of the parable of the sower, where the seed that fell on good soil grew and produced fruit, up to a hundred times what was sown.
Jesus says, 'He who has ears, let him hear!' – the same exhortation concluding the parable in Luke 8:8, an invitation to spiritual attentiveness.
Mark's parallel where Jesus says: 'He who has ears to hear, let him hear!' – corresponding to the conclusion in Luke 8:8.
Matthew's parallel: 'He who has ears, let him hear!' – the same exhortation concluding the parable of the sower.
In Revelation, the expression is used: 'He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches' – the same motif of having ears to hear.
Isaiah prophesies about the people's condition: they hear but do not understand – a background Jesus uses for the formulation 'he who has ears to hear'.

The parable of the sower's good soil and hundredfold fruit points to the richness of the fruit of faith. Ruth's loyalty as a Moabite woman illustrates that whoever receives God's word in good soil bears rich fruit.
Jesus says that whoever remains in him bears much fruit – thematically parallel to the fertility of the good soil in the parable of the sower.
The fruit of the Spirit is described by Paul – a parallel to the spiritual fruitfulness represented by the good soil in the parable.
Paul prays that the Colossians may bear fruit in every good work – thematically linked to bearing fruit a hundredfold in good soil.
